Below is a practical, evidence-backed workflow to correlate two types of soil classification. “Correlate” can mean (i) translate or map categories between systems so they align spatially, and/or (ii) quantify how strongly two categorical soil classifications co-vary or agree across an area (e.g., USDA texture vs FAO hydrologic groups, Soil Taxonomy vs WRB, or two digital soil maps from different frameworks). The steps below combine cross-walking, statistics, and GIS methods.

1) Clarify goals and choose a target relationship
- Decide whether you want exact taxonomic equivalence (e.g., map USDA soil texture classes to FAO/UNESCO texture classes), predictive correlation (e.g., predict WRB orders from Soil Taxonomy using attributes), or pattern-level association (e.g., how often a WRB order co-occurs with a USDA texture class in the landscape). <cite id="60672de5-0">Multiple soil classification frameworks are used in practice for different roles (e.g., FAO-UNESCO for soil class distribution and USDA/NRCS for textural class assignment), so cross-walking between systems is common</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">Even when taxonomic systems differ (USDA vs WRB), the recorded types of soil information per category can be largely compatible, enabling cross-system correlation</cite>.

2) Assemble data and align scales
- Collect attribute data or maps for both classification schemes. For texture, USDA/NRCS uses sand/silt/clay fractions to assign 13 textural classes via a triangle; FAO/UNESCO commonly uses a reduced set of 7 hydrologic texture classes or broader soil classes with coarse/medium/fine descriptors. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA/NRCS soil texture assigns classes from sand, silt, and clay proportions using the texture triangle with 13 classes</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-4">FAO soil texture files often use 7 texture classes and coarse/medium/fine descriptors based on clay content for regional mapping</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD provides image maps linked to attributes including texture for top and subsoils, enabling reclassification into hydrologic groups</cite>.
- Ensure spatial alignment. If maps are at different scales or resolutions, reproject and resample; where necessary, simplify or aggregate legend entries to make categories comparable. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Grouping similar mapping units into a simplified legend improved reproduction of the original map and allowed evaluation of accuracy changes via error matrices and Kappa</cite>.

3) Build a cross-walk: exact translation or attribute-driven mapping
- Texture classes: Use numeric thresholds to translate between USDA/NRCS and FAO/UNESCO. For example, USDA class boundaries are defined by sand/silt/clay content and can be used to assign FAO texture bins; many studies map USDA classes onto USCS/FAO texture groupings with explicit tables. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA/NRCS provides explicit class boundaries by texture fraction, enabling direct assignment of texture classes</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-2">USDA classes can be grouped into broader USCS texture classes/groups and overlaid visually, with counts summarized for training/testing</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Soil texture classes defined by USDA/NRCS can be further analyzed to assign structure and permeability classes via published guidelines, illustrating attribute-driven cross-walking</cite>.
- Taxonomic families/orders and WRB: Where taxonomies differ (USDA Soil Taxonomy vs WRB), align by known equivalences (e.g., order-level families) and by soil property patterns; studies often document such correlations explicitly. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">Field-identified USDA Taxonomy units (e.g., Haplustepts, Haplustalfs, Terriorthents) correlated to WRB Luvisols, Arenosols, and Fluvisols, providing an example of cross-taxonomic classification mapping</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">Despite different taxonomic systems, the information recorded per category (e.g., depth, rock fragments, conductivity) can be aligned to maintain compatibility</cite>.
- GIS implementation: Reclassify layers using cross-walk tables or field calculators; for continuous attributes (e.g., sand %), apply thresholds to assign classes; use zonal or polygon join to transfer classes between layers. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Erodibility mapping workflows use zonal statistics and USDA-derived texture classes combined with FAO/UNESCO structure/permeability codes, demonstrating attribute transfer and reclassification in ArcGIS</cite>.

4) Quantify association and agreement across the landscape
- Contingency tables and overall association: Build a cross-tabulation (error matrix) between the two classified maps or between translated classes. Use overall accuracy, producer/user accuracy per class, and Kappa to quantify agreement beyond chance. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Map accuracy is commonly assessed via error matrices with overall accuracy, producer accuracy, user accuracy, and Cohen’s Kappa to correct for chance agreement</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa is widely used to compare soil maps because it compares correct allocations to expected chance and is supported by established literature; strength-of-agreement ranges are commonly applied</cite>.
- Statistical tests: For two categorical classifications, use chi-square (or likelihood ratio) to test independence and Cramér’s V for effect size; logistic regression models with indicator variables can test whether one classification predicts the other and estimate odds ratios per class shift. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Legend reclassification and stratification can change accuracy metrics (overall accuracy, Kappa), illustrating how cross-walking and grouping affect agreement diagnostics</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Goodness-of-fit tests (Pearson chi-square, deviance) and logistic regression criteria (log-likelihood, odds ratios, Z tests) are used to select and validate models predicting soil mapping unit occurrence, extending to cross-classification prediction</cite>.
- Predictive cross-walk (optional): If you want to translate one map into the other probabilistically, train a multiclass classifier or GLM using co-located labels. <cite id="70ab7c62-3">Random Forest and Multinomial Logistic Regression have been compared for predicting soil orders; differences in Kappa show the value of predictive validation when comparing classifications</cite>.

5) Validate and refine with an independent sample
- Use stratified sampling or temporally independent areas to validate the cross-walk and correlation. Report overall accuracy, Kappa, and per-class user/producer accuracy to diagnose where mismatches concentrate. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Stratifying by hydrologic class (e.g., drainage) altered overall accuracy and Kappa and revealed specific over/under-classification patterns, guiding refinement of the cross-walk</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa and associated significance testing provide consistent, reproducible comparisons between source and predicted (or cross-walked) maps</cite>.

6) Practical examples and templates
- Texture-based correlation: Translate USDA/NRCS classes to FAO hydrologic texture using USDA sand/silt/clay thresholds; reclassify a HWSD layer into FAO classes; compare with an existing FAO layer using an error matrix and Kappa. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA texture triangle provides class boundaries for direct translation</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD layers can be reclassified into hydrologic groups for cross-system comparison</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Structure/permeability codes mapped per USDA texture class further validate texture-to-function consistency</cite>.
- Taxonomy-to-WRB mapping: For each soil unit, record both USDA and WRB labels; build a small cross-walk linking orders/families to WRB orders based on properties and horizons; where ambiguous, expand sampling to horizon-level descriptions and texture; then compute agreement and covariation. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">USDA units matched to WRB in a case study showed clear correspondences (e.g., Haplustepts→Luvisols), enabling cross-classification</cite>.
- Joint hydrologic grouping: Collapse both schemes into a small number of hydrologic or agricultural groups (A–D) to maximize correlation at the landscape scale when taxonomies differ substantially. <cite id="60672de5-3">US soil maps have been reclassified into A–D hydrologic groups for consistent landscape analysis</cite>.

7) GIS workflow to correlate and overlay soil maps from different systems
- Data preparation: Ensure both layers share a common coordinate system; if needed, aggregate or simplify categories to match the coarser legend. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Simplifying or grouping mapping units into a reduced legend can improve predictive capacity and ease overlay</cite>.
- Attribute joins and reclassification: Use spatial joins or zonal statistics to transfer attributes; apply cross-walk tables to translate category codes; for continuous pedologic attributes (e.g., sand %), apply consistent thresholds per system. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Zonal statistics with USDA texture classes and structure/permeability codes demonstrate attribute transfer and statistical summarization across polygons</cite>.
- Joint classification: Compute a joint probability table (P(a,b)) for paired categories; derive conditional probabilities P(a|b) and P(b|a); identify dominant misclassifications and homogeneity regions. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Error matrices compare estimated and original maps pixel-by-pixel to compute overall accuracy, producer/user accuracy, and Kappa, which extend directly to joint classification diagnostics</cite>.
- Visualization and diagnostics: Choropleth both the original and cross-walked maps; highlight disagreements; compute landscape pattern metrics (e.g., Shannon diversity of joint classes) to summarize correlation strength. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Accuracy gains/losses after stratified reclassification reveal spatial patterns of error and correlation</cite>.

8) Reporting and uncertainty management
- Report both global and local metrics: overall accuracy, Kappa, and per-class user/producer accuracies; include a contingency table and, if modeling, model-odds ratios for class transitions. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa is a standard metric for thematic map comparison and is interpreted via Landis & Koch ranges</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Producer and user accuracy and log-likelihood tests support transparent model selection and validation</cite>.
- Document cross-walk rationale: provide tables mapping USDA/NRCS to FAO/USCS or USDA Taxonomy to WRB with field evidence and attribute rules; note scale/resolution mismatches and how they were handled. <cite id="60672de5-4">Even with compatible recorded properties, differences in scale and additional properties (e.g., depth, rock fragments) require explicit handling in cross-system correlation</cite>.
- Sensitivity analysis: Repeat cross-walking with alternative thresholds or legend groupings to show robustness. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Grouping and stratification choices altered overall accuracy and Kappa, illustrating sensitivity to classification granularity</cite>.

Illustrative case combining these steps
- Scenario: You have a USDA NRCS texture-mapped soil layer and an FAO-based regional soil map. Correlation plan: 
  1) Use USDA texture triangle thresholds to translate each USDA polygon into an FAO texture class; reclassify the FAO map to a reduced 4-class hydrologic group (A–D) for landscape consistency. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA triangle thresholds underpin the translation</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD-style reclassification into hydrologic groups A–D is a common standard</cite>. 
  2) Build an error matrix between the translated USDA layer and the FAO layer; compute overall accuracy and Kappa. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Error matrices and Kappa are standard for such comparisons</cite>. 
  3) If discrepancies are high in certain texture bins, fit a simple logistic model predicting FAO class from USDA texture and clay content to refine the cross-walk. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Goodness-of-fit and logistic regression criteria support model selection and adjustment</cite>. 
  4) Validate on an independent area and report per-class user/producer accuracy and confusion matrix to diagnose persistent errors. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa and associated interpretation provide robust validation</cite>.

Limitations and when to choose each method
- Exact taxonomic equivalence is rare across systems; rely on cross-walk tables, field correlations, and attribute logic. <cite id="60672de5-4">USDA vs WRB units may align functionally even if formal names differ; mapping the same property set enables correlation</cite>. 
- Global association vs local heterogeneity: Use Kappa/accuracy for big-picture correlation; use joint-classification heatmaps to find local mismatches. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Heatmap-level errors (e.g., underestimation of MU68, overestimation of MU1) reveal spatial drivers</cite>. 
- If the goal is predictive mapping rather than historical correlation, train a model with co-located labels and validate with Kappa and cross-validation. <cite id="70ab7c62-3">Predictive comparisons (e.g., RF vs MLR) show substantial Kappa differences, underscoring the need for proper model validation</cite>.

Summary checklist
- Document the two classification systems and their intended use; select target metrics (Kappa, overall accuracy, Cramér’s V, etc.). <cite id="60672de5-0">Different frameworks serve different roles; document roles to choose appropriate cross-walking</cite>. 
- Build a defensible cross-walk (tables, field correlations, attribute rules) and implement in GIS. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">Texture triangle thresholds support translation</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">USDA Taxonomy to WRB correspondences can be documented and applied</cite>. 
- Quantify agreement with error matrices and Kappa; explore covariation via contingency tables and logistic regression. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa standardizes agreement beyond chance</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Logistic regression and error matrix metrics support robust evaluation</cite>. 
- Validate on independent data and iterate cross-walk rules; visualize joint-classification to diagnose spatial drivers of mismatch. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Stratification and reclassification diagnostics reveal spatial patterns of error</cite>. 
- Report both global and local findings, with clear cross-walk tables and metrics, and note limitations due to scale/resolution and taxonomic differences. <cite id="60672de5-4">Taxonomic differences can be compatible in recorded properties, but scale and missing attributes require explicit handling</cite>.

Open gaps and how to resolve them
- Formal cross-walk catalogs: Some official cross-walks (e.g., full Soil Taxonomy to WRB) are maintained by agencies; consult national soil surveys and recent comparative mapping papers to extract tables and rules and calibrate local cross-walks. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">Case-study cross-walks provide concrete exemplars to bootstrap local tables</cite>. 
- Texture thresholds across regions: Although USDA thresholds are universal, local pedogenesis can shift apparent texture–property relationships; include local calibration samples when building predictive cross-walks. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Model selection and goodness-of-fit tests ensure local relevance of predictive cross-walks</cite>.

With these steps, you can reliably correlate two soil classification systems either for one-off mapping alignment or for quantitative assessment of their landscape-scale association. <cite id="60672de5-0">Different frameworks are often complementary and can be integrated in analysis</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">When systems record similar properties, compatibility is often high enough to support robust cross-correlation with careful cross-walking and validation</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa-based agreement and error-matrix accuracy provide defensible, reportable metrics</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence-backed workflow to correlate two types of soil classification. “Correlate” can mean (i) translate or map categories between systems so they align spatially, and/or (ii) quantify how strongly two categorical soil classifications co-vary or agree across an area (e.g., USDA texture vs FAO hydrologic groups, Soil Taxonomy vs WRB, or two digital soil maps from different frameworks). The steps below combine cross-walking, statistics, and GIS methods.

1) Clarify goals and choose a target relationship
- Decide whether you want exact taxonomic equivalence (e.g., map USDA soil texture classes to FAO/UNESCO texture classes), predictive correlation (e.g., predict WRB orders from Soil Taxonomy using attributes), or pattern-level association (e.g., how often a WRB order co-occurs with a USDA texture class in the landscape). <cite id="60672de5-0">Multiple soil classification frameworks are used in practice for different roles (e.g., FAO-UNESCO for soil class distribution and USDA/NRCS for textural class assignment), so cross-walking between systems is common</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">Even when taxonomic systems differ (USDA vs WRB), the recorded types of soil information per category can be largely compatible, enabling cross-system correlation</cite>.

2) Assemble data and align scales
- Collect attribute data or maps for both classification schemes. For texture, USDA/NRCS uses sand/silt/clay fractions to assign 13 textural classes via a triangle; FAO/UNESCO commonly uses a reduced set of 7 hydrologic texture classes or broader soil classes with coarse/medium/fine descriptors. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA/NRCS soil texture assigns classes from sand, silt, and clay proportions using the texture triangle with 13 classes</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-4">FAO soil texture files often use 7 texture classes and coarse/medium/fine descriptors based on clay content for regional mapping</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD provides image maps linked to attributes including texture for top and subsoils, enabling reclassification into hydrologic groups</cite>.
- Ensure spatial alignment. If maps are at different scales or resolutions, reproject and resample; where necessary, simplify or aggregate legend entries to make categories comparable. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Grouping similar mapping units into a simplified legend improved reproduction of the original map and allowed evaluation of accuracy changes via error matrices and Kappa</cite>.

3) Build a cross-walk: exact translation or attribute-driven mapping
- Texture classes: Use numeric thresholds to translate between USDA/NRCS and FAO/UNESCO. For example, USDA class boundaries are defined by sand/silt/clay content and can be used to assign FAO texture bins; many studies map USDA classes onto USCS/FAO texture groupings with explicit tables. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA/NRCS provides explicit class boundaries by texture fraction, enabling direct assignment of texture classes</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-2">USDA classes can be grouped into broader USCS texture classes/groups and overlaid visually, with counts summarized for training/testing</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Soil texture classes defined by USDA/NRCS can be further analyzed to assign structure and permeability classes via published guidelines, illustrating attribute-driven cross-walking</cite>.
- Taxonomic families/orders and WRB: Where taxonomies differ (USDA Soil Taxonomy vs WRB), align by known equivalences (e.g., order-level families) and by soil property patterns; studies often document such correlations explicitly. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">Field-identified USDA Taxonomy units (e.g., Haplustepts, Haplustalfs, Terriorthents) correlated to WRB Luvisols, Arenosols, and Fluvisols, providing an example of cross-taxonomic classification mapping</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">Despite different taxonomic systems, the information recorded per category (e.g., depth, rock fragments, conductivity) can be aligned to maintain compatibility</cite>.
- GIS implementation: Reclassify layers using cross-walk tables or field calculators; for continuous attributes (e.g., sand %), apply thresholds to assign classes; use zonal or polygon join to transfer classes between layers. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Erodibility mapping workflows use zonal statistics and USDA-derived texture classes combined with FAO/UNESCO structure/permeability codes, demonstrating attribute transfer and reclassification in ArcGIS</cite>.

4) Quantify association and agreement across the landscape
- Contingency tables and overall association: Build a cross-tabulation (error matrix) between the two classified maps or between translated classes. Use overall accuracy, producer/user accuracy per class, and Kappa to quantify agreement beyond chance. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Map accuracy is commonly assessed via error matrices with overall accuracy, producer accuracy, user accuracy, and Cohen’s Kappa to correct for chance agreement</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa is widely used to compare soil maps because it compares correct allocations to expected chance and is supported by established literature; strength-of-agreement ranges are commonly applied</cite>.
- Statistical tests: For two categorical classifications, use chi-square (or likelihood ratio) to test independence and Cramér’s V for effect size; logistic regression models with indicator variables can test whether one classification predicts the other and estimate odds ratios per class shift. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Legend reclassification and stratification can change accuracy metrics (overall accuracy, Kappa), illustrating how cross-walking and grouping affect agreement diagnostics</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Goodness-of-fit tests (Pearson chi-square, deviance) and logistic regression criteria (log-likelihood, odds ratios, Z tests) are used to select and validate models predicting soil mapping unit occurrence, extending to cross-classification prediction</cite>.
- Predictive cross-walk (optional): If you want to translate one map into the other probabilistically, train a multiclass classifier or GLM using co-located labels. <cite id="70ab7c62-3">Random Forest and Multinomial Logistic Regression have been compared for predicting soil orders; differences in Kappa show the value of predictive validation when comparing classifications</cite>.

5) Validate and refine with an independent sample
- Use stratified sampling or temporally independent areas to validate the cross-walk and correlation. Report overall accuracy, Kappa, and per-class user/producer accuracy to diagnose where mismatches concentrate. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Stratifying by hydrologic class (e.g., drainage) altered overall accuracy and Kappa and revealed specific over/under-classification patterns, guiding refinement of the cross-walk</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa and associated significance testing provide consistent, reproducible comparisons between source and predicted (or cross-walked) maps</cite>.

6) Practical examples and templates
- Texture-based correlation: Translate USDA/NRCS classes to FAO hydrologic texture using USDA sand/silt/clay thresholds; reclassify a HWSD layer into FAO classes; compare with an existing FAO layer using an error matrix and Kappa. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA texture triangle provides class boundaries for direct translation</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD layers can be reclassified into hydrologic groups for cross-system comparison</cite>. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Structure/permeability codes mapped per USDA texture class further validate texture-to-function consistency</cite>.
- Taxonomy-to-WRB mapping: For each soil unit, record both USDA and WRB labels; build a small cross-walk linking orders/families to WRB orders based on properties and horizons; where ambiguous, expand sampling to horizon-level descriptions and texture; then compute agreement and covariation. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">USDA units matched to WRB in a case study showed clear correspondences (e.g., Haplustepts→Luvisols), enabling cross-classification</cite>.
- Joint hydrologic grouping: Collapse both schemes into a small number of hydrologic or agricultural groups (A–D) to maximize correlation at the landscape scale when taxonomies differ substantially. <cite id="60672de5-3">US soil maps have been reclassified into A–D hydrologic groups for consistent landscape analysis</cite>.

7) GIS workflow to correlate and overlay soil maps from different systems
- Data preparation: Ensure both layers share a common coordinate system; if needed, aggregate or simplify categories to match the coarser legend. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Simplifying or grouping mapping units into a reduced legend can improve predictive capacity and ease overlay</cite>.
- Attribute joins and reclassification: Use spatial joins or zonal statistics to transfer attributes; apply cross-walk tables to translate category codes; for continuous pedologic attributes (e.g., sand %), apply consistent thresholds per system. <cite id="dcad8d84-1">Zonal statistics with USDA texture classes and structure/permeability codes demonstrate attribute transfer and statistical summarization across polygons</cite>.
- Joint classification: Compute a joint probability table (P(a,b)) for paired categories; derive conditional probabilities P(a|b) and P(b|a); identify dominant misclassifications and homogeneity regions. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Error matrices compare estimated and original maps pixel-by-pixel to compute overall accuracy, producer/user accuracy, and Kappa, which extend directly to joint classification diagnostics</cite>.
- Visualization and diagnostics: Choropleth both the original and cross-walked maps; highlight disagreements; compute landscape pattern metrics (e.g., Shannon diversity of joint classes) to summarize correlation strength. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Accuracy gains/losses after stratified reclassification reveal spatial patterns of error and correlation</cite>.

8) Reporting and uncertainty management
- Report both global and local metrics: overall accuracy, Kappa, and per-class user/producer accuracies; include a contingency table and, if modeling, model-odds ratios for class transitions. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa is a standard metric for thematic map comparison and is interpreted via Landis & Koch ranges</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Producer and user accuracy and log-likelihood tests support transparent model selection and validation</cite>.
- Document cross-walk rationale: provide tables mapping USDA/NRCS to FAO/USCS or USDA Taxonomy to WRB with field evidence and attribute rules; note scale/resolution mismatches and how they were handled. <cite id="60672de5-4">Even with compatible recorded properties, differences in scale and additional properties (e.g., depth, rock fragments) require explicit handling in cross-system correlation</cite>.
- Sensitivity analysis: Repeat cross-walking with alternative thresholds or legend groupings to show robustness. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Grouping and stratification choices altered overall accuracy and Kappa, illustrating sensitivity to classification granularity</cite>.

Illustrative case combining these steps
- Scenario: You have a USDA NRCS texture-mapped soil layer and an FAO-based regional soil map. Correlation plan: 
  1) Use USDA texture triangle thresholds to translate each USDA polygon into an FAO texture class; reclassify the FAO map to a reduced 4-class hydrologic group (A–D) for landscape consistency. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">USDA triangle thresholds underpin the translation</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-3">HWSD-style reclassification into hydrologic groups A–D is a common standard</cite>. 
  2) Build an error matrix between the translated USDA layer and the FAO layer; compute overall accuracy and Kappa. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Error matrices and Kappa are standard for such comparisons</cite>. 
  3) If discrepancies are high in certain texture bins, fit a simple logistic model predicting FAO class from USDA texture and clay content to refine the cross-walk. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Goodness-of-fit and logistic regression criteria support model selection and adjustment</cite>. 
  4) Validate on an independent area and report per-class user/producer accuracy and confusion matrix to diagnose persistent errors. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Cohen’s Kappa and associated interpretation provide robust validation</cite>.

Limitations and when to choose each method
- Exact taxonomic equivalence is rare across systems; rely on cross-walk tables, field correlations, and attribute logic. <cite id="60672de5-4">USDA vs WRB units may align functionally even if formal names differ; mapping the same property set enables correlation</cite>. 
- Global association vs local heterogeneity: Use Kappa/accuracy for big-picture correlation; use joint-classification heatmaps to find local mismatches. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Heatmap-level errors (e.g., underestimation of MU68, overestimation of MU1) reveal spatial drivers</cite>. 
- If the goal is predictive mapping rather than historical correlation, train a model with co-located labels and validate with Kappa and cross-validation. <cite id="70ab7c62-3">Predictive comparisons (e.g., RF vs MLR) show substantial Kappa differences, underscoring the need for proper model validation</cite>.

Summary checklist
- Document the two classification systems and their intended use; select target metrics (Kappa, overall accuracy, Cramér’s V, etc.). <cite id="60672de5-0">Different frameworks serve different roles; document roles to choose appropriate cross-walking</cite>. 
- Build a defensible cross-walk (tables, field correlations, attribute rules) and implement in GIS. <cite id="dcad8d84-0">Texture triangle thresholds support translation</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">USDA Taxonomy to WRB correspondences can be documented and applied</cite>. 
- Quantify agreement with error matrices and Kappa; explore covariation via contingency tables and logistic regression. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa standardizes agreement beyond chance</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Logistic regression and error matrix metrics support robust evaluation</cite>. 
- Validate on independent data and iterate cross-walk rules; visualize joint-classification to diagnose spatial drivers of mismatch. <cite id="70ab7c62-0">Stratification and reclassification diagnostics reveal spatial patterns of error</cite>. 
- Report both global and local findings, with clear cross-walk tables and metrics, and note limitations due to scale/resolution and taxonomic differences. <cite id="60672de5-4">Taxonomic differences can be compatible in recorded properties, but scale and missing attributes require explicit handling</cite>.

Open gaps and how to resolve them
- Formal cross-walk catalogs: Some official cross-walks (e.g., full Soil Taxonomy to WRB) are maintained by agencies; consult national soil surveys and recent comparative mapping papers to extract tables and rules and calibrate local cross-walks. <cite id="70ab7c62-2">Case-study cross-walks provide concrete exemplars to bootstrap local tables</cite>. 
- Texture thresholds across regions: Although USDA thresholds are universal, local pedogenesis can shift apparent texture–property relationships; include local calibration samples when building predictive cross-walks. <cite id="70ab7c62-4">Model selection and goodness-of-fit tests ensure local relevance of predictive cross-walks</cite>.

With these steps, you can reliably correlate two soil classification systems either for one-off mapping alignment or for quantitative assessment of their landscape-scale association. <cite id="60672de5-0">Different frameworks are often complementary and can be integrated in analysis</cite>. <cite id="60672de5-4">When systems record similar properties, compatibility is often high enough to support robust cross-correlation with careful cross-walking and validation</cite>. <cite id="70ab7c62-1">Kappa-based agreement and error-matrix accuracy provide defensible, reportable metrics</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: For each prediction method, a set of best fit regressions was selected based on criteria as goodness to fit tests (Pearson and deviance), log-likelihood, odds ratio, and Z test (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 1989). A set of logistic regressions was determined for the unstratified prediction method, and two sets of logistic regressions were selected for the stratified prediction method, respectively for well drained areas and for poorly drained areas. These sets of logistic regressions were used to estimate the probabilities of occurrence of each soil mapping unit. These sets of equations were organized as scripts in ArcView 3.2 environment, assigning a probability value to each pixel for the entire study area and creating eight maps, each of them representing for the entire study area the probability of occurrence of each soil mapping unit. Using the function Map Query of ArcView Spatial Analyst Extension on the probability maps, two soil maps were estimated (one for stratified and one for not stratified procedures) by assigning to every single pixel the denomination of the soil mapping unit that had the larger probability of occurrence on that pixel. 

The accuracy of the estimated soil maps was determined by using error matrices (Congalton, 1991) comparing all pixels of the estimated maps to the original soil map, by this way using a larger dataset than in the training points dataset, and intending to evaluate what would be the effects of using logistic regressions for extrapolating prediction of soil occurrence to other areas than only the training points. For each prediction method, a set of best fit regressions was selected based on criteria as goodness to fit tests (Pearson and deviance), log-likelihood, odds ratio, and Z test (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 1989). A set of logistic regressions was determined for the unstratified prediction method, and two sets of logistic regressions were selected for the stratified prediction method, respectively for well drained areas and for poorly drained areas. Using the function Map Query of ArcView Spatial Analyst Extension on the probability maps, two soil maps were estimated (one for stratified and one for not stratified procedures) by assigning to every single pixel the denomination of the soil mapping unit that had the larger probability of occurrence on that pixel. 

The accuracy of the estimated soil maps was determined by using error matrices (Congalton, 1991) comparing all pixels of the estimated maps to the original soil map, by this way using a larger dataset than in the training points dataset, and intending to evaluate what would be the effects of using logistic regressions for extrapolating prediction of soil occurrence to other areas than only the training points. Below is a practical workflow to correlate USCS and AASHTO classifications using only Atterberg limits (LL, PL, PI = LL−PL), along with evidence-backed decision rules, examples, and caveats.

Summary of what can be inferred from LL and PL
- Both AASHTO and USCS primarily use LL and PL (and PI) to distinguish coarse- from fine-grained behavior and to separate granular from silt–clay materials when the fine fraction dominates. <cite id="22d9e517-2">AASHTO explicitly uses particle-size analysis and Atterberg limits, with tables as guides</cite> and <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS uses particle size to split coarse-grained versus fine-grained soils, and for fines relies on the Casagrande plasticity chart without subdividing sand</cite>. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">Feature-importance analyses show that the fines fraction (F200), LL, and PI are key variables determining AASHTO group assignment</cite>.

1) AASHTO classification from LL and PL (no grain-size distribution)
- Determine fines content if possible. If sieve data are missing, you can still use the Atterberg-based “fine fraction” concept qualitatively: if PI is low and LL−PL is small, the material behaves like low-plasticity sand/gravel; if PI is high and LL is large, it behaves like silt–clay. <cite id="22d9e517-2">AASHTO uses Atterberg limits with a table as a guide to classify soils even when only particle-size and Atterberg data are available</cite>. 
- Use the AASHTO plasticity chart to anchor subgroup boundaries:
  - Compute PI = LL − PL. Plot LL vs PI on the Casagrande chart; classify the fine fraction as A-4/A-5 (low-plasticity granular) versus A-6/A-7 (high-plasticity cohesive) using the A-line and liquidity index concepts. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL thresholds (≤40 vs >40) help separate low- vs high-plasticity groups (e.g., A-4/A-5 vs A-6/A-7), and the PI distinguishes between A-2-4/A-2-5 and A-2-6/A-2-7 subgroups</cite>. 
- Assign groups without sieve percentages by using AASHTO Table 211.1-style logic:
  - If the material is dominantly coarse-grained (by engineering judgment or available context) and LL is low, assign A-1–A-3 per AASHTO; if LL−PL is small and PI≤10, assign A-2-4; if LL−PL increases and exceeds typical sands, move to A-2-6. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Field examples show A-2-4, SM and A-2 assignments based on LL/PL behavior and standard practice</cite>. 
  - If the material is dominantly fine-grained and PI is very high with LL large (e.g., LL≈85, PL≈35, PI≈50), classify as A-7-5; such points lie well above the A-line on the plasticity chart. <cite id="22d9e517-4">An example reports LL=80.16, PL=35.72, PI=44.44 and assigns A-7-5; the same work notes A-7-5 corresponds to PI>(LL−30)</cite>.

Snippet: Soil classification systems (SCS) play a critical role in predicting the behavior and response of soils in various engineering and construction applications. As noted by ref. [20], "Soil classification enables the engineer to assign a soil to one of a limited number of groups, based on the material properties and characteristics of the soil". Indeed, the properties and characteristics used for soil classification encompass various factors, such as textural, chemical, mineralogical, physical, and geotechnical attributes. Commonly, soil classification systems categorize soils into various behavioral categories based on their particle size distribution and Atterberg limits, which relate to their plasticity. There are several widely recognized soil classification systems in use, each with its own set of criteria and terminology. Some of the common soil classification systems include British Standards (BS), The American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials (AASHTO) classification, The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) (ASTM D2487) and Australian Standards (AS). 

In accordance with ASTM and AASHTO standards, soils classified as coarse-grained are defined as those in which no more than 35% and 50%, respectively, of the particles pass through the number 200 sieve (0.075 mm). Grain size distribution-based classification systems are commonly utilized for coarse-grained soils, encompassing materials such as gravel and thoroughly washed sands. In soils containing a substantial proportion of fines, specifically silt and clay particles, the nature and amount of clay minerals within the soil take on significant importance [21]. For fine-grained or cohesive soils, Atterberg limits or plasticity characteristics are primarily used to classify and predict their behavior. According to [22], "Atterberg limits are known to reflect the combined effects of soil constituents and their interaction with the pore fluid." Table 1 displays the particle size ranges that are associated with gravel, sand, silt, and clay fractions. The table indicates that there are variations in the particle size range for gravel, sand, silt, and clay among commonly used standards. In the USCS standard, soils that are finer than 0.075 mm (sand particles) are not subdivided, but instead, the use of the Casagrande plasticity chart is relied upon for distinguishing silty and clayey soils.
</snippet>

Title: AI-Enhanced Soil Classification Using Machine Learning Models within the AASHTO Framework
Snippet: AASHTO classification is determined using a combination of gradation and plasticity data. The parameters represent the essential physical and index properties required for distinguishing granular soils from fine-grained silt-clay materials, and for determining subgroup boundaries. The selected parameters and their roles are summarized as Table 2. 

Gradation-related parameters, including the percentages passing intermediate sieves (e.g., No. 10 and No. 40), are used to distinguish among granular subgroups. These gradation characteristics affect drainage, density, and load-bearing performance, making them essential for accurate subgroup identification within the granular soil classes [32,33]. F200 represents the proportion of soil particles finer than 0.075 mm and is the most critical factor in AASHTO classification. It determines the primary division between granular soils (≤35% fines) and silt-clay soils (>35% fines). Feature-importance analysis from the RF model confirmed that F200 is the most influential variable among all inputs, exerting the strongest control on group assignment [11,34]. Liquid limit represents the moisture content at which a soil changes from plastic behavior to liquid-like flow. Within the AASHTO system, LL is used to differentiate low-plasticity soils (LL ≤ 40) from high-plasticity soils (LL > 40), particularly for identifying transitions between groups such as A-4 and A-5, and between A-6 and A-7. LL also contributes to distinguishing the two subgroups A-7-5 and A-7-6 [35,36]. 

PI quantifies the plasticity of the fine fraction and is a key determinant in differentiating silty and clayey behavior. Soils with PI ≤ 10 are classified as silty, whereas PI ≥ 11 indicates clayey fines. PI strongly influences subgroup boundaries within the A-2 class (e.g., A-2-4/A-2-5 vs. A-2-6/A-2-7). In the model robustness tests, omission of PI led to a notable reduction in classification accuracy, further confirming the importance of plasticity behavior in AASHTO categorization [35,37].

Below is a practical workflow to correlate USCS and AASHTO classifications using only Atterberg limits (LL, PL, PI = LL−PL), along with evidence-backed decision rules, examples, and caveats.

Summary of what can be inferred from LL and PL
- Both AASHTO and USCS primarily use LL and PL (and PI) to distinguish coarse- from fine-grained behavior and to separate granular from silt–clay materials when the fine fraction dominates. <cite id="22d9e517-2">AASHTO explicitly uses particle-size analysis and Atterberg limits, with tables as guides</cite> and <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS uses particle size to split coarse-grained versus fine-grained soils, and for fines relies on the Casagrande plasticity chart without subdividing sand</cite>. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">Feature-importance analyses show that the fines fraction (F200), LL, and PI are key variables determining AASHTO group assignment</cite>.

1) AASHTO classification from LL and PL (no grain-size distribution)
- Determine fines content if possible. If sieve data are missing, you can still use the Atterberg-based “fine fraction” concept qualitatively: if PI is low and LL−PL is small, the material behaves like low-plasticity sand/gravel; if PI is high and LL is large, it behaves like silt–clay. <cite id="22d9e517-2">AASHTO uses Atterberg limits with a table as a guide to classify soils even when only particle-size and Atterberg data are available</cite>. 
- Use the AASHTO plasticity chart to anchor subgroup boundaries:
  - Compute PI = LL − PL. Plot LL vs PI on the Casagrande chart; classify the fine fraction as A-4/A-5 (low-plasticity granular) versus A-6/A-7 (high-plasticity cohesive) using the A-line and liquidity index concepts. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL thresholds (≤40 vs >40) help separate low- vs high-plasticity groups (e.g., A-4/A-5 vs A-6/A-7), and the PI distinguishes between A-2-4/A-2-5 and A-2-6/A-2-7 subgroups</cite>. 
- Assign groups without sieve percentages by using AASHTO Table 211.1-style logic:
  - If the material is dominantly coarse-grained (by engineering judgment or available context) and LL is low, assign A-1–A-3 per AASHTO; if LL−PL is small and PI≤10, assign A-2-4; if LL−PL increases and exceeds typical sands, move to A-2-6. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Field examples show A-2-4, SM and A-2 assignments based on LL/PL behavior and standard practice</cite>. 
  - If the material is dominantly fine-grained and PI is very high with LL large (e.g., LL≈85, PL≈35, PI≈50), classify as A-7-5; such points lie well above the A-line on the plasticity chart. <cite id="22d9e517-4">An example reports LL=80.16, PL=35.72, PI=44.44 and assigns A-7-5; the same work notes A-7-5 corresponds to PI>(LL−30)</cite>. 
- Practical rule for missing sieve data: 
  - If PI≤10 and LL is not suspiciously high, treat as low-plasticity granular (A-2-4 or A-2-5 depending on gradation), else treat as cohesive (A-2-6/A-2-7 or A-6/A-7) using LL and PI to bracket the plasticity chart boundaries. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL and PI jointly determine subgroup boundaries; PI≥11 typically indicates clayey fines and shifts classification within the A-2 family</cite>. 
- Example from literature: Lateritic soil with LL=44, PL=41, PI=3 showed A-6 behavior on AASHTO, consistent with low plasticity and dominantly cohesive fines; another lateritic soil with LL=29.08, PL=17.36, PI=11.72 and 1.43% passing No. 200 was assigned A-2-6(0). <cite id="22d9e517-1">LL=44, PL=41, PI=3 → A-6</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-3">LL=29.08, PL=17.36, PI=11.72 with 1.43% <200 → A-2-6(0)</cite>. 
- Caveat on PL measurement: Ensure PL is reliable; small PL biases can flip chart-side assignment. <cite id="6a9bc473-1">Using a standardized PL procedure reduces classification inconsistencies; discrepancies occur mainly for points near the A-line, underscoring sensitivity of LL–PL-based boundaries</cite>.

2) USCS classification from LL and PL (no grain-size distribution)
- Separate coarse- vs fine-grained control:
  - If the material exhibits granular behavior (low plasticity, PI small, and no evidence of cohesive fines), assign to GW/GM/GC/GMB using LL/PI to infer clay/silt presence; sand dominance with minimal fines → GW/GM. <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS does not subdivide sand by size below 0.075 mm; plasticity chart is used only to distinguish silty vs clayey fines, so low PI with small LL implies granular behavior</cite>. 
  - If the material exhibits cohesive behavior and >50% fines are inferred or strongly suspected (from high LL and PI), classify the fine fraction using the USCS “MH/MC/CH” rule: if PI is high and LL is large, treat as CH; if PI small but LL not extremely low, treat as MH or OC depending on organic content. <cite id="167154e3-1">A soil with LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 was classified as CH in USCS, consistent with A-7-5 in AASHTO</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-4">LL=80, PL=36, PI=44 → CH in USCS and A-7-5 in AASHTO</cite>. 
- Plasticity-chart heuristics for fines when only LL and PL are available:
  - Use the Casagrande chart to infer “silty vs clayey” fines:
    - If LL is low and PI≤10, the fines are silty (MH or GM if sands are present); if PI≥11 and LL is moderate–high, the fines are clayey (MC or CH). <cite id="6a9bc473-3">For fine-grained or cohesive soils, Atterberg limits are used; the USCS plasticity chart distinguishes silty and clayey soils without subdividing sand</cite> <cite id="6a9bc473-4">PI≤10 indicates silty fines; PI≥11 indicates clayey fines within AASHTO logic, which aligns with USCS MH/MC/CH thresholds</cite>. 
  - For ambiguous LL–PI (near A-line), collect corroborative tests (e.g., natural moisture content, shrinkage limit, or organic tests) to resolve whether the soil is predominantly silty or clayey. <cite id="6a9bc473-1">Soils near the A-line are most sensitive to PL measurement and chart interpretation; two misclassifications out of 84 occurred only for points close to the A-line</cite>. 
- Correlate to USCS group letters using LL/PI without sieve:
  - If LL−PL is very low and material is granular-looking, assign GW/GM (no clayey fines) or GC if cohesive traces exist but PI is small; if LL−PL is moderate and PI increases, move to GM/MH or GC/MC; if LL−PL is high and LL is large, assign CH. <cite id="167154e3-0">Empirical correlations show PL and LL are predictive of compaction features and strongly influence classification; higher PL (and to some extent LL) indicate cohesive behavior</cite>. 
  - Example mapping: LL≈29, PL≈17, PI≈12 with only 1.43% <200 → A-2-6(0) in AASHTO suggests fine-grained cohesive behavior, which maps to USCS MC or CH depending on fines dominance; conversely, LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 maps to CH in USCS. <cite id="22d9e517-3">LL=29.08, PL=17.36, PI=11.72 with 1.43% <200 → A-2-6(0)</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 → USCS CH</cite>. 
- When sieve data are truly unavailable:
  - Group by dominant behavior:
    - Nonplastic to low-plasticity with sand-like feel and PI≤10 → GW/GM or GM (if no coarse fraction evidence) or A-2-4 in AASHTO; if cohesive traces present but minor → GC/MC.
    - High plasticity and large LL → CH or MC if significant fines and organic matter; check for organic odor/behavior to justify MO or MH. <cite id="22d9e517-0">AASHTO/USCS classifications in practice for subgrade soils show A-2-4, SM ↔ A-2 and A-2-4, SM ↔ A-1 depending on non-plastic behavior; these align with low-PI, sand-like behavior</cite>. 
    - Transitional LL–PI (e.g., LL≈40–50, PI≈10–20) → GM/MH or A-2-4/A-2-5; LL>50 and PI>20 with A-line above → A-7-5/CH. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL>40 separates low- from high-plasticity groups; PI governs A-2 subgrouping</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-4">PI>(LL−30) is a rule-of-thumb for A-7-5</cite>. 
  - If organic content is suspected (strong odor, black color, low LL with high liquidity), classify as MO or MH with appropriate AASHTO A-6/A-4 overlap if LL and PI are not diagnostic. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Soils exhibiting non-plastic behavior and classifying as A-1 (USDA) while AASHTO assigns A-2-4/SM illustrate the role of organic and textural diagnostics when Atterberg limits are the only data</cite>. 

3) Correlating the two systems via LL/PL
- Build a direct bridge using plasticity-derived behavior:
  - Fine-grained cohesive with LL>50 and PI>20, plotting above the A-line → AASHTO A-7-5 and USCS CH. <cite id="22d9e517-4">LL=80, PL=36, PI=44 → A-7-5 (AASHTO) and CH (USCS)</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 → A-7-5 and CH</cite>. 
  - Low- to moderate-plasticity fines with PI≤10 → AASHTO A-2-4 or A-2-5 and USCS GM/MH or A-2 (granular) if sand dominates. <cite id="22d9e517-0">AASHTO A-2-4, SM and USCS A-2 overlap for low-plasticity subgrades</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-1">LL=44, PL=41, PI=3 → A-6 (AASHTO) aligns with cohesive fines; low PI suggests silty-clay borderline</cite>. 
  - Granular-like behavior with LL≤40 and PI≤10 → AASHTO A-2-4 or A-1–A-3 and USCS GW/GM/GC. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL≤40 indicates low-plasticity granular behavior used to separate A-4/A-5 from A-6/A-7</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-0">Field examples show A-2-4, SM and A-2 across systems for low-plasticity subgrade soils</cite>. 
- Use AASHTO Table 211.1-style decision logic when only LL/PL are available:
  - If F200 is low/unknown but LL and PI indicate granular behavior → A-2-4 or A-1–A-3; if LL and PI indicate cohesive fines → A-2-6/A-2-7 or A-6/A-7. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">F200 is the primary division; LL and PI refine subgroup choice within A-2 and between A-6/A-7</cite>. 
  - If F200 is high (>50%) and LL/PI show cohesive behavior → USCS MH/CH or MC; AASHTO A-6/A-7 or A-2-6. <cite id="22d9e517-3">A-2-6(0) indicates >35% fines and cohesive behavior</cite> <cite id="167154e3-4">USCS CH corresponds to AASHTO A-7-5 for cohesive, high-LL/PI materials</cite>. 
- Cross-check with USDA textural triangle when possible:
  - Use LL and PL to infer likely USDA textural class (e.g., silt/clay) and then map to USCS and AASHTO group letters accordingly. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Case studies mapped subgrade soils across AASHTO, ASTM/USCS, and USDA using Atterberg limits and routine testing</cite>. 

4) Handling edge cases and ambiguities with only LL/PL
- Organic soils and highly expansive clays:
  - If organic odor/feel and high plasticity coexist (LL high, PI high, strong volume change), classify AASHTO A-6 or A-7-5 and USCS MO or CH; reserve CH/MC only when mineralogy and test confirm significant clay content. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Soils classified as A-2 (USCS) but A-1 (USDA) illustrate the role of organic and textural diagnostics when Atterberg limits are the only data</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">High LL/PI expansive soils map to A-7-5 and CH</cite>. 
- Boundary cases near the A-line:
  - Expect higher uncertainty. If two adjacent group boundaries are within the measurement error (e.g., PI≈10–12, LL≈40–45), collect natural water content or do a small sieve/hydrometer check to decide between silty vs clayey, or report both possibilities with ranges. <cite id="6a9bc473-1">Most inconsistencies arise when points lie near the A-line; standardized PL and LL testing improves confidence</cite>. 
- Sands with trace fines:
  - LL≈25–40 and PI≈0–5 suggest GW/GM or GM; avoid assigning GC/MC without corroborating cohesion tests. <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS uses plasticity only to separate silty vs clayey fines; small PI supports granular assignment</cite>. 

5) Practical workflow to correlate AASHTO and USCS from LL and PL only
- Step 1: Compute PI = LL − PL. Record test uncertainties.
  - If LL and PL are far from boundaries (e.g., LL≤30, PI≤5) → likely granular; if LL≥50, PI≥20 → likely cohesive. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL and PI thresholds help separate low- vs high-plasticity categories that govern group selection</cite>. 
- Step 2: Estimate fines fraction qualitatively:
  - If material feels/behaves granular and PI is low, assume ≤35% fines (coarse-grained) for AASHTO; if cohesive and PI high, assume >35% fines (fine-grained). <cite id="6a9bc473-4">F200 is the primary split in AASHTO; LL/PI refine group within A-2 and A-6/A-7</cite>. 
- Step 3: Assign AASHTO subgroup:
  - Granular with LL≤40 and PI≤10 → A-2-4 or A-2-5; cohesive with LL>40 and PI>20 → A-7-5; intermediate cases use the plasticity chart to pick A-2-6/A-2-7 or A-6/A-7. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL>40 separates A-4/A-5 from A-6/A-7; PI distinguishes A-2-4/A-2-5 vs A-2-6/A-2-7</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-4">A-7-5 when PI>(LL−30)</cite>. 
- Step 4: Assign USCS group:
  - Coarse-grained dominant with low PI → GW/GM/GC/GMB; fine-grained dominant with high LL/PI → CH/MC; transitional LL/PI → GM/MH or GC/MC; ambiguous LL/PI → use additional diagnostics or report both likely USCS letters and justify with LL/PI ranges. <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS relies on size split and plasticity chart for silty/clayey fines; sand is not subdivided below 0.075 mm</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">High LL/PI map to CH</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-4">High LL/PI map to A-7-5 ↔ CH</cite>. 
- Step 5: Cross-validate with examples:
  - Low-PI, low-LL → A-2-4 (AASHTO) and A-2/GM (USCS). <cite id="22d9e517-0">A-2-4, SM and A-2 overlap for low-plasticity subgrade soils</cite>. 
  - High-LL, high-PI → A-7-5 (AASHTO) and CH (USCS). <cite id="22d9e517-4">LL=80, PL=36, PI=44 → A-7-5 and CH</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 → CH</cite>. 
  - Mixed cases with small %<200 → A-2-6(0) (AASHTO) and MC/CH (USCS) depending on cohesive feel. <cite id="22d9e517-3">LL=29.08, PL=17.36, PI=11.72 with 1.43% <200 → A-2-6(0)</cite>. 
- Step 6: Document assumptions and uncertainties:
  - State whether fines fraction was assumed coarse-grained vs fine-grained and how LL/PI proximity to chart boundaries affects confidence. <cite id="6a9bc473-1">Classification discrepancies concentrate near A-line; standardizing limit tests reduces uncertainty</cite>. 

6) Accuracy and limitations when only Atterberg limits are available
- Strengths: LL and PL capture plasticity and liquidity thresholds that drive subgroup boundaries for both systems, especially for fine-grained soils; LL and PI jointly explain much of the variability in AASHTO group assignment. <cite id="6a9bc473-4">Model analyses show F200, LL, and PI dominate AASHTO classification accuracy</cite>. 
- Limitations: LL/PL alone cannot resolve sand versus silt/clay fractions cleanly; overlap regions (LL≈40–50, PI≈10–20) are common sources of cross-system mismatch unless corroborated by sieve/hydrometer or organic tests. <cite id="6a9bc473-3">USCS uses plasticity only to separate silty vs clayey fines; sand is not subdivided</cite> <cite id="6a9bc473-1">A-line proximity increases ambiguity</cite>. 
- Practical resolution: If grain-size data are truly unavailable, combine domain context (dominant aggregates observed, borrow material), repeat LL/PL tests, and, if subgrade performance matters, run a quick hydrometer on a small split sample to resolve silt/clay proportions. <cite id="22d9e517-0">Field classifications across AASHTO, ASTM/USCS, and USDA using Atterberg limits exemplify how context plus limits can assign practical groups</cite>. 

Examples that demonstrate cross-system mapping from LL/PL
- A-2-4 ↔ A-2 and SM overlap: low-plasticity subgrade with LL≈35–40, PL≈30–32, PI≈5–10; AASHTO assigns A-2-4/SM while USCS assigns A-2 or GM depending on sand dominance. <cite id="22d9e517-0">SG1 classified A-2-4, SM (AASHTO), A-2 (USCS); SG2 A-2-4, SM (AASHTO), A-1 (USCS), reflecting non-plastic behavior and textural differences</cite>. 
- A-6 vs A-7-5/CH: LL≈44, PL≈41, PI≈3 → A-6 (AASHTO); LL≈80–94, PL≈36–40, PI≈44–54 → A-7-5 (AASHTO) and CH (USCS). <cite id="22d9e517-1">LL=44, PL=41, PI=3 → A-6</cite> <cite id="22d9e517-4">LL=80.16, PL=35.72, PI=44.44 → A-7-5 and CH</cite> <cite id="167154e3-1">LL=94, PL=40, PI=54 → A-7-5 and CH</cite>. 
- Transitional A-2-6(0) ↔ MC/CH: LL≈29, PL≈17, PI≈12 with only 1.43% passing No. 200 → A-2-6(0) in AASHTO; cohesive feel suggests MC or CH in USCS. <cite id="22d9e517-3">LL=29.08, PL=17.36, PI=11.72, 1.43% <200 → A-2-6(0)</cite>. 

In practice
- Build a small lookup table for your project’s soils: list LL, PL, PI, assumed %<200, provisional AASHTO group per Table 211.1 logic, provisional USCS letter per plasticity heuristics, and a note on uncertainty. Use this to map borrow, subgrade, and embankment soils across systems, and revisit if sieve/hydrometer data become available. <cite id="22d9e517-2">AASHTO classification uses tables as guides with Atterberg limits</cite> <cite id="6a9bc473-4">LL and PI refine group selection within A-2 and A-6/A-7</cite>. 
- For critical earthworks, consider running minimal additional tests (e.g., one hydrometer run per sample) to lift ambiguous cases from LL/PL alone. <cite id="6a9bc473-1">Improving PL/LL measurement reduces misclassification near chart boundaries</cite>.

Title: An appraisal of the problems related to the application of Casagrande Plasticity Chart and Unified Soil Classification System in classifying lateritic soils in Nigeria
Snippet: Soil classification systems (SCS) play a critical role in predicting the behavior and response of soils in various engineering and construction applications. As noted by ref. [20], "Soil classification enables the engineer to assign a soil to one of a limited number of groups, based on the material properties and characteristics of the soil". Indeed, the properties and characteristics used for soil classification encompass various factors, such as textural, chemical, mineralogical, physical, and geotechnical attributes. Commonly, soil classification systems categorize soils into various behavioral categories based on their particle size distribution and Atterberg limits, which relate to their plasticity. There are several widely recognized soil classification systems in use, each with its own set of criteria and terminology. Some of the common soil classification systems include British Standards (BS), The American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials (AASHTO) classification, The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) (ASTM D2487) and Australian Standards (AS). 

In accordance with ASTM and AASHTO standards, soils classified as coarse-grained are defined as those in which no more than 35% and 50%, respectively, of the particles pass through the number 200 sieve (0.075 mm). Grain size distribution-based classification systems are commonly utilized for coarse-grained soils, encompassing materials such as gravel and thoroughly washed sands. In soils containing a substantial proportion of fines, specifically silt and clay particles, the nature and amount of clay minerals within the soil take on significant importance [21]. For fine-grained or cohesive soils, Atterberg limits or plasticity characteristics are primarily used to classify and predict their behavior. According to [22], "Atterberg limits are known to reflect the combined effects of soil constituents and their interaction with the pore fluid." Table 1 displays the particle size ranges that are associated with gravel, sand, silt, and clay fractions. The table indicates that there are variations in the particle size range for gravel, sand, silt, and clay among commonly used standards. In the USCS standard, soils that are finer than 0.075 mm (sand particles) are not subdivided, but instead, the use of the Casagrande plasticity chart is relied upon for distinguishing silty and clayey soils.

Title: AI-Enhanced Soil Classification Using Machine Learning Models within the AASHTO Framework
Snippet: AASHTO classification is determined using a combination of gradation and plasticity data. The parameters represent the essential physical and index properties required for distinguishing granular soils from fine-grained silt-clay materials, and for determining subgroup boundaries. The selected parameters and their roles are summarized as Table 2. 

Gradation-related parameters, including the percentages passing intermediate sieves (e.g., No. 10 and No. 40), are used to distinguish among granular subgroups. These gradation characteristics affect drainage, density, and load-bearing performance, making them essential for accurate subgroup identification within the granular soil classes [32,33]. F200 represents the proportion of soil particles finer than 0.075 mm and is the most critical factor in AASHTO classification. It determines the primary division between granular soils (≤35% fines) and silt-clay soils (>35% fines). Feature-importance analysis from the RF model confirmed that F200 is the most influential variable among all inputs, exerting the strongest control on group assignment [11,34]. snippet.text:
Soil classification systems (SCS) play a critical role in predicting the behavior and response of soils in various engineering and construction applications. As noted by ref. [20], "Soil classification enables the engineer to assign a soil to one of a limited number of groups, based on the material properties and characteristics of the soil". Indeed, the properties and characteristics used for soil classification encompass various factors, such as textural, chemical, mineralogical, physical, and geotechnical attributes. Commonly, soil classification systems categorize soils into various behavioral categories based on their particle size distribution and Atterberg limits, which relate to their plasticity. There are several widely recognized soil classification systems in use, each with its own set of criteria and terminology. Some of the common soil classification systems include British Standards (BS), The American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials (AASHTO) classification, The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) (ASTM D2487) and Australian Standards (AS). 

In accordance with ASTM and AASHTO standards, soils classified as coarse-grained are defined as those in which no more than 35% and 50%, respectively, of the particles pass through the number 200 sieve (0.075 mm). Grain size distribution-based classification systems are commonly utilized for coarse-grained soils, encompassing materials such as gravel and thoroughly washed sands. In soils containing a substantial proportion of fines, specifically silt and clay particles, the nature and amount of clay minerals within the soil take on significant importance [21]. For fine-grained or cohesive soils, Atterberg limits or plasticity characteristics are primarily used to classify and predict their behavior. According to [22], "Atterberg limits are known to reflect the combined effects of soil constituents and their interaction with the pore fluid." Table 1 displays the particle size ranges that are associated with gravel, sand, silt, and clay fractions. The table indicates that there are variations in the particle size range for gravel, sand, silt, and clay among commonly used standards. In the USCS standard, soils that are finer than 0.075 mm (sand particles) are not subdivided, but instead, the use of the Casagrande plasticity chart is relied upon for distinguishing silty and clayey soils.
